text: Roman religion was the faith of ancient Rome, in Italy, from more than 2,500 to about 1,600 years ago.
According to legend, Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome, gave it its calendar and its priests.
src: Roman religion was the polytheistic religion of ancient Rome / the city of Rome in Italy / years: -509 to 391
legend credited Aeneas, Romulus and above all Numa Pompilius, the Sabine second king of Rome, with its rites, calendar and priesthoods

text: The Romans worshipped many gods, such as Jupiter, the most powerful, and Minerva.
They gave the gods prayers and offerings and asked for help in return: “I give that you might give.”
src: the polytheistic religion of ancient Rome / Jupiter, the most powerful / a Capitoline temple to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva
prayer, vow and sacrifice were exchanged with the gods on the principle of do ut des, “I give that you might give” / Vows promised offerings in return for benefits

text: Rome's priests were usually important men who also ran the government, such as Julius Caesar.
Six women, the Vestals, tended the sacred fire of the state, and every family honoured its own household gods.
src: Priesthoods were held by the elite, often by the same men who held political office / Julius Caesar became pontifex maximus in 63 BCE
the six Vestals tended the sacred hearth of the state and every household honoured its own Lares and Penates / the Vestals’ sacred fire

text: As Rome grew, it welcomed the gods of other peoples instead of getting rid of them.
Traders and soldiers brought home gods from faraway lands, such as the goddess Cybele and the god Mithras.
src: As Rome grew, its policy was to absorb the gods and cults of other peoples rather than root them out
traders and legions brought home cults from Egypt, Greece, Iberia, India and Persia, among them those of Cybele, Isis, Mithras and Sol Invictus

text: It had no holy book: what mattered was saying the prayers and doing the rituals exactly right.
Much of what we know comes from Roman writers, like Vergil, who wrote the Aeneid.
src: Roman religion had no scripture / It depended on knowing and correctly performing prayer, rite and sacrifice / the words had to be exact
Much is known through writers / Vergil’s Aeneid gave the Imperial vision of the past

text: After Christians had long been persecuted, Christianity became the empire's religion and Emperor Theodosius I ended support for the old gods.
Yet some old festivals lived on for a long time, and Christian holidays were fitted into the old calendar.
src: Christians were persecuted / Nicene Christianity became the empire’s official religion / Theodosius I ends official support for all other cults
Christian festivals were fitted into the old calendar / the Lupercalia was celebrated as late as the 5th century
